title: SHE DIDN’T HAVE THE PULPIT. BUT SHE KNEW THE TRUTH HE WAS MISSING.
paragraphs: SHE DIDN’T HAVE THE PULPIT. BUT SHE KNEW THE TRUTH HE WAS MISSING.

The untold power of Priscilla, the woman who helped a gifted preacher understand the way of God more accurately—and why her story still confronts every Christian who thinks knowing Scripture is the same as knowing Christ.
He could preach.

He could reason from the Scriptures. He could hold the attention of a room. He had the education, the eloquence, the confidence, and the kind of passion that made people stop what they were doing and listen.
There was just one problem.
He didn't know everything he needed to know.
And somewhere in the congregation sat a woman who recognized what was missing.
She could have embarrassed him.
She could have publicly challenged him, made an example of his incomplete understanding, or quietly dismissed him as another confident religious voice who needed correcting.
But she didn't.
Instead, she and her husband did something so beautiful, so humble, and so spiritually mature that the Holy Spirit preserved it in Scripture for generations to read.
They took him aside.
And they explained the way of God more accurately.
Her name was Priscilla.

And if you have ever felt that your contribution to God's kingdom was too small, your voice too ordinary, your past too complicated, or your place too insignificant to matter, you need to understand what happened in Acts 18.
Because this story is not simply about a woman who knew her Bible.
It is about what happens when truth meets humility, when knowledge becomes discipleship, and when God uses people who are more interested in building His kingdom than building their own reputation.
But there is something else here.
Something uncomfortable.
Something that might expose the difference between the Christianity we display and the Christianity we actually live.
And it begins with a man named Apollos.
Acts 18:24–25 introduces him as a Jewish man from Alexandria who arrived in Ephesus. He was eloquent, competent in the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, and fervent in spirit.
He spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus.
Read that carefully.
Accurately.
Luke does not describe Apollos as a fraud, an enemy of Christ, or a man deliberately deceiving people.
He was sincere. He was knowledgeable. He was passionate. He had received genuine instruction.
But his understanding was incomplete.
Acts 18:25 says he knew only the baptism of John.
John the Baptist had preached repentance and prepared Israel for the coming Messiah. His baptism pointed people toward the One who was coming after him.
But the Christian proclamation could not stop at preparation.
Jesus Christ had come.
He had been crucified for sins. He had risen from the dead. He had been exalted as Lord. And the promised Holy Spirit had been poured out upon His people.
Luke does not tell us precisely which details Apollos had yet to understand. We must not pretend to know what Scripture does not reveal.
What we do know is that Apollos needed a fuller explanation of God's way.
And God placed Priscilla and Aquila in his path.
Not to destroy him.
To help him grow.
That distinction matters more than many of us realize.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christians began confusing correction with humiliation.
We learned how to win arguments but forgot how to restore people.
We learned how to identify theological mistakes but sometimes neglected the gentleness required to help someone understand the truth.
We became skilled at exposing what others did not know while becoming strangely resistant to anyone exposing what we ourselves still needed to learn.
And then we encounter Priscilla.
A woman whose quiet act of discipleship asks every one of us a question:
Do you love the truth enough to receive correction—and do you love people enough to correct them without crushing them?
Before we go further, we need to know who this woman actually was.
Priscilla, also called Prisca, was a Jewish Christian woman married to Aquila, a Jewish man originally from Pontus.

Acts 18:2–3 tells us that Aquila and Priscilla had come from Italy after Emperor Claudius ordered Jews to leave Rome. Paul encountered them in Corinth and stayed and worked with them because they shared the same trade: tentmaking.
Imagine that for a moment.
A husband and wife uprooted from their home.
Their ordinary life interrupted by an imperial decree.
The uncertainty of relocation. The need to rebuild. The exhausting work of making a living somewhere else.
Scripture does not tell us everything they felt, what they lost, or how they processed that disruption.
But it tells us enough to see that their story included displacement and a new beginning.
And in Corinth, their path crossed with the apostle Paul.
What looked like an unwanted relocation became part of a remarkable story of Christian fellowship and ministry.
That does not mean every painful displacement is secretly a blessing in disguise, or that God approves of the injustice that causes suffering.
It means that suffering does not place a person beyond God's ability to work.
Some of you know what it feels like to have your plans overturned.
You worked for stability, and everything changed.
You prayed for one door to open, and instead another closed.
You thought your life was finally becoming predictable, and suddenly you were rebuilding from the beginning.
Priscilla's story does not promise that every disruption will end in visible success.
It reminds us that a changed address does not cancel our calling to faithfulness.
You can lose your familiar surroundings without losing your place in God's purposes.
And Priscilla did not need a public platform to become useful in those purposes.
She worked.
She traveled.
She served alongside her husband.
She participated in the life and mission of the early church.
And when the moment came to help Apollos, she was ready.
Acts 18:26 records the encounter.
In the Greek text, the crucial phrase reads:
ἀκριβέστερον αὐτῷ ἐξέθεντο τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ θεοῦ
akribesteron autō exethento tēn hodon tou theou
A faithful translation is:
“They explained to him the way of God more accurately.”
That word, ἀκριβέστερον (akribesteron), is the comparative form of a word expressing accuracy or precision.
More accurately.
Not more aggressively.
Not more dramatically.
Not more impressively.
More accurately.
The Greek verb ἐξέθεντο (exethento) communicates the act of explaining or setting something forth.
And notice the plural verb.
They explained.
Priscilla and Aquila.
Together.
Luke explicitly includes both husband and wife in this work of helping Apollos understand God's way.
The text does not tell us exactly which words Priscilla spoke or how much of the explanation came from either spouse. It would be dishonest to invent a conversation that Scripture does not record.
But it would be equally dishonest to erase her participation.
She was there.
She was named.
She helped explain.
And the Holy Spirit, who inspired Scripture, did not consider her contribution unworthy of remembrance.
There is another detail that deserves attention.
Luke names her before Aquila in Acts 18:26.
In several other passages, including Romans 16:3 and 2 Timothy 4:19, her name also appears first.

Scholars have suggested several possible reasons for this ordering, including her prominence or recognized contribution to ministry. But the text does not explicitly explain why her name sometimes comes first.
We should not build more upon the order than Scripture allows.
What we can say with confidence is that Priscilla was a respected Christian coworker who actively participated in teaching Apollos.
And that alone should make us think.
How many people have we overlooked because they did not look like our idea of a significant servant of God?
How many faithful believers have served quietly while everyone watched the person holding the microphone?
How many men and women have strengthened churches through hospitality, patient instruction, prayer, encouragement, generosity, and years of unseen sacrifice?
Not everyone is called to the same role.
Christians also differ in how they understand the relationship between this passage and other New Testament teachings about church leadership and teaching authority.
But those discussions must not obscure what Acts 18 plainly says.
Priscilla, alongside Aquila, helped a gifted man understand God's way more accurately.
Her contribution mattered.
And the way she made that contribution is just as important as the fact that she made it.
Acts 18:26 says Apollos began to speak boldly in the synagogue.
Priscilla and Aquila heard him.
Then they took him aside.
The Greek expression προσελάβοντο αὐτόν (proselabonto auton) conveys taking him to themselves or receiving him into their company.
Luke does not describe a public confrontation or a spectacle.
He describes a personal encounter.
Think about how different that is from the culture many of us have learned to accept.
Someone says something incomplete.
Someone else notices.
Within minutes, the disagreement becomes a performance.
Screenshots.
Accusations.
Mockery.
An audience gathering to watch someone be dismantled.
And somehow we convince ourselves that because we are defending truth, every method we use must be justified.
But biblical truth never gives us permission to abandon biblical love.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Galatians 6:1 teaches that those who are spiritual should restore someone caught in transgression with a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves.
And 2 Timothy 2:24–25 describes the Lord's servant as someone who must not be quarrelsome, but kind, able to teach, and patient, correcting opponents with gentleness.
These passages do not forbid necessary public correction. Scripture itself sometimes requires public rebuke, especially when public wrongdoing or harmful teaching demands it.
But Acts 18 shows us something precious.
A situation where personal instruction served the truth without making humiliation the goal.
Priscilla and Aquila did not need to make Apollos look small in order to make God's truth clear.
And there is a second lesson here that may be even harder to receive.
Apollos listened.
At least, the narrative presents him continuing in ministry after their instruction, without describing resistance or rejection.
Imagine his position.
He was educated.
He was eloquent.
He knew the Scriptures.
He was already speaking boldly in the synagogue.
And then two fellow believers took him aside to explain what he had not yet fully understood.
He could have treated the conversation as an insult.
He could have allowed pride to protect his ignorance.
He could have insisted that his knowledge was sufficient because his ministry was already attracting attention.
But the story moves forward with Apollos continuing to serve.
Acts 18:27–28 tells us that when he wished to go to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him.
When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed.
He powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
Do you see the beauty?
The man who needed further instruction became a great help to others.
The correction did not end his usefulness.
It became part of the story of his continued service.
And this is where the passage stops being a distant account of first-century Christians and begins speaking directly to us.
Because there is an Apollos in many of us.
We know enough Scripture to sound convincing.
We have been Christians long enough to recognize familiar verses.
We can explain doctrines, debate interpretations, and identify errors in other people's beliefs.
But can we still be taught?
Can we admit when our understanding is incomplete?
Can we receive correction from someone we did not expect God to use?
Can we say, without defensiveness, “I need to study that more carefully”?
Or have we become so attached to appearing spiritually mature that we are afraid to admit we are still growing?
There is a dangerous kind of pride that hides behind biblical knowledge.
It does not always look arrogant.
Sometimes it looks like certainty that refuses examination.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to apologize because we believe our intentions were good.
Sometimes it looks like quoting Scripture to silence someone whose correction we do not want to hear.
And sometimes it looks like knowing the language of grace while treating other people with contempt.
That is not the maturity Christ calls us to.
First Corinthians 8:1 warns that knowledge can puff up, while love builds up.
Knowledge matters. Doctrine matters. Accuracy matters.
Priscilla and Aquila did not dismiss Apollos's incomplete understanding as unimportant.
They helped him understand more accurately precisely because the truth mattered.
But truth was not a trophy to display.
It was a gift to steward faithfully.
And Apollos was not an enemy to defeat.
He was a fellow servant to strengthen.
The goal of Christian correction is not to prove that we are superior. It is to serve the truth of Christ and the good of His people.
Perhaps you are reading this while remembering a time someone corrected you.
Maybe they were right, but the way they spoke wounded you.
Maybe they embarrassed you in front of people you respected.
Maybe you stopped asking questions because you were afraid of being made to feel foolish.
If that happened, the wound deserves to be acknowledged.
But do not allow someone's unkindness to convince you that growing in biblical understanding is dangerous.
The answer to harsh correction is not refusing all correction.
The answer is learning to recognize truth, receive it humbly, and practice it with love.
Or perhaps you are remembering someone you corrected.
A child.
A spouse.
A fellow believer.
A new Christian who was still learning.
You knew the answer.
But now, remembering the conversation, you realize that your words may have communicated superiority more than love.
You wanted them to recognize the truth.
But did you help them recognize the heart of Christ?
That question is worth sitting with.
Because we can be factually correct and relationally careless.
We can defend a biblical position while failing to display the patience Scripture commands.
And we can become so focused on exposing error that we forget the person standing in front of us is someone God calls us to love.
Priscilla's example invites us to something better.
Not compromise.
Not silence.
Not pretending that every interpretation is equally faithful to Scripture.
But courage joined with gentleness.
Conviction joined with humility.
Accuracy joined with love.
And all of it submitted to Jesus Christ.
There is one more detail about Priscilla that makes her story even richer.
Her service did not end with Apollos.
In Romans 16:3–4, Paul calls Prisca and Aquila his fellow workers in Christ Jesus and says they risked their necks for his life.
He expresses gratitude to them, adding that the churches of the Gentiles also give thanks.
The exact circumstances of that danger are not recorded.
We cannot responsibly invent a dramatic rescue scene or claim to know how they risked their lives.
But Paul's words are unmistakable.
Their commitment to Christ and His people had cost them something.
And in Romans 16:5, Paul also greets the church meeting in their house.
First Corinthians 16:19 likewise refers to Aquila and Prisca and the church in their house.
Their home was not merely a private refuge from the world.
It became a place where believers gathered.
Think about that.
The same couple who shared ordinary work with Paul also opened their home for Christian fellowship and helped instruct a gifted teacher.
They served through labor, hospitality, instruction, partnership, and costly faithfulness.
Their ministry was not confined to a single moment.
It was woven into the ordinary fabric of their lives.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may never preach before thousands.
You may never write a bestselling Christian book.
You may never have a public ministry, a recognizable name, or an audience applauding your faithfulness.
But you can open your home.
You can explain a passage of Scripture to someone who is confused.
You can encourage a believer who is ready to give up.
You can teach your children the Gospel.
You can help a friend recognize a misunderstanding.
You can pray with someone who has run out of words.
You can support faithful Christian work without needing public recognition.
You can remain steady when no one is watching.
And none of that is insignificant simply because it is unseen.
Jesus taught in Matthew 6 that our Father sees what is done in secret.
That does not mean every private act of service will produce visible success.
It means our faithfulness is not measured by public attention.
And the story of Priscilla reminds us that a quiet act of instruction can have consequences beyond what the people involved could have imagined.
Yet we must be careful about where we place the glory.
Priscilla was not the Savior.
Aquila was not the Savior.
Apollos was not the Savior.
Paul was not the Savior.
Jesus Christ was—and is—the Savior.
That is the center of this story.
The way of God that Apollos needed to understand more accurately ultimately leads us to the person and work of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not merely a call to become more educated, more eloquent, or more morally impressive.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for our sins and was raised from the dead.
As Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.
That is not a minor detail in Christian teaching.
It is the heart of the message.
And if we speak beautifully about faith while neglecting the crucified and risen Christ, our message has lost its center.
If we teach repentance without pointing people to the grace of Christ, we leave them staring at their guilt without showing them the Savior.
If we speak about grace while refusing Christ's call to repentance, we distort the very grace we claim to celebrate.
The Gospel calls sinners to turn to God through Jesus Christ, trusting in His saving work rather than their own goodness.
It announces forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life through Him.
And that is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Because the deepest scandal in the human story is not that imperfect people sometimes misunderstand Scripture.
It is that sinners have rebelled against a holy God.
And the astonishing grace of the Gospel is that God has acted in Jesus Christ to save those who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 declares that God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we had mastered theology.
Not after we had cleaned up every hidden failure.
Not after we had finally become worthy of His attention.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
But mercy that meets us in our guilt and calls us into a new life.
And if Christ has shown us such mercy, how can we treat every person who needs correction as though they are beyond patience?
How can we refuse to admit our own need for instruction?
How can we celebrate forgiveness on Sunday and spend the rest of the week refusing to forgive?
The Gospel does not merely change what we believe about salvation.
It should change the way we speak, listen, correct, repent, serve, and love.
That is why Priscilla's story matters.
She reminds us that truth is worth explaining carefully.
Apollos reminds us that gifted believers still have room to grow.
Aquila reminds us that faithful partnership can strengthen the work of the Gospel.
And together, their story points us beyond human personalities to the Lord whose truth they sought to serve.
Maybe you are the person who has been quietly studying Scripture, wondering whether God could ever use you.
Keep learning.
Keep growing.
Remain faithful.
You do not need to manufacture a platform to become a servant of Christ.
Maybe you are the person who has been speaking confidently but privately knows there are things you have never taken time to examine.
Do not be afraid to learn.
The ability to admit what you do not know is not spiritual defeat.
It can be the beginning of deeper understanding.
Maybe you are the person who has used truth like a weapon and now realizes someone was hurt by the way you handled it.
There is grace for repentance.
You can acknowledge what was wrong.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can learn to speak with greater care.
And maybe you are the person who has spent years feeling invisible.
You have served.
You have prayed.
You have given.
You have helped people who may never remember what you did for them.
Do not measure your worth by whether anyone applauds.
Your identity is not found in being noticed.
For those who belong to Christ, it is found in belonging to Him.
And now, before you leave this story, consider one question.
What if the person God is using to help you grow is someone you have been too proud to listen to?
Not every correction is true.
Not every confident religious voice is trustworthy.
Everything must be tested by Scripture, read carefully in context.
But when someone faithfully opens God's Word and helps you understand it more accurately, will you receive the truth?
Even if it exposes something you have believed for years?
Even if it requires you to apologize?
Even if it means admitting that passion alone is not enough?
Apollos had eloquence.
He had knowledge.
He had zeal.
But he still needed instruction.
And Priscilla, alongside Aquila, helped provide it.
The result was not the destruction of a promising servant.
The story continued with Apollos helping believers and demonstrating from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
What a beautiful picture of Christian discipleship.
Not a competition for who knows the most.
Not a battle for who receives the most attention.
But believers helping one another become more faithful to the truth of Jesus.
That is the kind of community we should desire.

A community where questions are welcomed, Scripture is handled carefully, repentance is taken seriously, grace is never cheapened, and no one is encouraged to confuse spiritual popularity with spiritual maturity.
A community where the person who teaches remains teachable.
Where the person who corrects remains humble.
Where the person who serves quietly is not treated as less important.
And where Jesus Christ receives the glory.
If this story has revealed something in your own heart, do not rush past it.
Perhaps you need to ask God to remove pride.
Perhaps you need courage to use the biblical understanding He has given you to help someone else.
Perhaps you need healing from a painful experience of correction.
Or perhaps you simply need to return to the Scriptures with the willingness to learn again.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly. A simple request for prayer is enough.
And if this passage has helped you understand something you had overlooked, share that insight. Your testimony may encourage another believer who is wrestling with the same question.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who believes their quiet service has no value.
Someone who feels disqualified because they are not eloquent.
Someone who has been wounded by harsh religious criticism.
Someone who knows the language of Christianity but has stopped growing in the Word.

Not because saving a post makes anyone more spiritual, but because there may come a day when you need to remember that faithful correction can be an act of love and that unseen service is still service.
Our desire is to keep pointing people back to Scripture, to repentance and grace, to the forgiveness found in Jesus Christ, and to a life of genuine discipleship.
And for those who want to help this work continue and grow, there is another invitation.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing another Christian article that disappears into a busy social media feed.
Our hope is to help people return to God's Word, understand it faithfully, and grow in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to encourage biblical understanding, spiritual nourishment, and practical Christian discipleship.
Keeping that work going takes time, care, resources, and the generosity of people who believe it is worth supporting.
Our first responsibility is faithfulness to Christ, not loyalty to any platform.
The apostle Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that each person should give as decided in the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Simply an opportunity to participate voluntarily in work that seeks to honor Jesus and serve His people.
These products are not the heart of the ministry. Christ is.
But they can be useful reminders, gifts, and resources that encourage faith and meaningful conversations about the Gospel.
You can still pray.
You can still invite others to study Scripture.
You can still use the free resources and encourage others to do the same.
And you can still serve Jesus faithfully right where He has placed you.
Priscilla's story should never become an excuse to measure spiritual worth by financial contributions or public recognition.
It teaches us the opposite.
The kingdom of God is served through faithful people using what they have received to strengthen others.
Some teach.
Some give.
Some encourage.
Some open their homes.
Some pray quietly.
Some make the Gospel known to a friend who has never understood it.
And all of us are called to remember that Christ is the head of His church.
If you choose to share, thank you for helping others discover it.
If you choose to pray, thank you for bringing this ministry before the Lord.
Whatever your part, may it be done freely, faithfully, and for the glory of God.
Because in the end, the story of Priscilla is not about a woman becoming famous.
It is about a woman and her husband faithfully helping someone understand the way of God.
It is about a gifted preacher who still needed to learn.
It is about believers strengthening believers.
And above all, it is about the Gospel of Jesus Christ being understood and proclaimed.
So the next time you feel insignificant because you are not the one speaking before the crowd, remember Priscilla.
And the next time you feel too knowledgeable to be corrected, remember Apollos.
The next time you are tempted to humiliate someone for what they do not yet understand, remember how this couple took him aside.
And the next time you wonder whether your small act of faithfulness matters, remember that God saw fit to preserve this moment in His Word.
A conversation.
A husband and wife.
A gifted man willing to receive fuller instruction.
And a Gospel worth understanding accurately.
May we be humble enough to learn, courageous enough to speak truth, gentle enough to restore, and faithful enough to serve when no one is watching.
And may every word we teach, every resource we share, every gift we offer, and every life we touch lead people not to our own importance, but to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the person who helps change the direction of someone's life is not the one standing before the crowd—but the one who loves them enough to quietly lead them closer to Jesus.
